pages.title: Introduction - The Linac: Workhorse of RT

content.text: Purpose: Why This Matters This lesson provides a detailed understanding of the linear accelerator (Linac), its primary components, their functions, and the Radiation Therapist's (RTT's) crucial role in its safe operation and daily quality assurance (QA).
Task: What You Will Do You will learn about the Linac's overall structure, how the radiation beam is produced and shaped, key safety features, and the operational checks RTTs perform daily.

Criteria for Success By the end of this lesson, you should be able to identify major Linac components, describe their purpose, explain basic emergency procedures for Linac operation, and understand the RTT's responsibilities for daily Linac QA.
The linear accelerator is the primary device used to deliver external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), precisely targeting tumors while sparing healthy tissue.
A medical linear accelerator is a complex system with several major sections working in concert.
Fig 1: Major Sections of a Linear Accelerator (Conceptual)
Drive Stand:
Typically fixed, contains components that generate and deliver microwave power to the gantry.
Gantry:
The large, rotating structure that houses the accelerator guide and treatment head; it directs the radiation beam towards the patient.
Treatment Couch (Patient Support Assembly - PSA):
Supports the patient and allows for precise positioning in multiple axes.
Control Console:
Located outside the treatment room, used by RTTs to set up, monitor, and deliver treatments.
Modulator Cabinet:
Contains components that distribute and monitor electrical power to the Linac, including the pulsed power supply for the microwave generator.
Objective Link: Knowing the "name of the treatment unit, beam characteristics including modality and energy" relates to understanding this system[cite: 1314].

pages.title: The Drive Stand - Powering the Beam

content.text: The drive stand is a crucial section, often secured to the floor, containing the primary components for generating the high-power microwaves needed to accelerate electrons.
Key Components in the Drive Stand:
Klystron (or Magnetron):
This is the microwave power source. A klystron is a linear-beam vacuum tube that amplifies microwaves, while a magnetron generates them. Most modern high-energy Linacs use klystrons.
Waveguide:
A system of hollow pipes that transports the high-power microwaves from the klystron/magnetron to the accelerator structure located in the gantry.
Circulator:
A device within the waveguide system that directs the RF energy flow and prevents microwaves from being reflected back into the klystron, which could damage it.
Water Cooling System:
Essential for dissipating the large amounts of heat generated by components like the accelerator structure, target, and klystron.
Quick Check: Which component in the drive stand is primarily responsible for generating or amplifying the microwave power used to accelerate electrons?
Check Answer
The gantry is the rotating part of the Linac that directs the radiation beam towards the patient.
Key Components in the Gantry:
Electron Gun:
Injects electrons into the accelerator structure.
Accelerator Structure (Waveguide):
A series of microwave cavities where electrons are accelerated to near the speed of light.
Bending Magnet:
Bends the electron beam (typically 90 or 270 degrees) to direct it towards the patient (or target for X-ray production).
Treatment Head:
Contains components to shape, modify, and monitor the beam (detailed on next page).
The
isocenter
is the fixed point in space around which the gantry, collimator, and couch rotate. It is typically 100 cm from the radiation source[cite: 1316].
The treatment head modifies the beam after it exits the accelerator structure. For photon therapy:
X-ray Target:
High-energy electrons strike this heavy metal target (e.g., tungsten) to produce X-rays via Bremsstrahlung.
Primary Collimator:
Shapes the beam after the target.
Beam-Flattening Filter:
A conical metal filter that makes the X-ray beam intensity more uniform across the field.
Ion Chambers:
Monitor the beam's dose rate, integrated dose, and flatness/symmetry.
Secondary Collimators (Jaws):
Movable heavy metal jaws (X and Y pairs) that define the rectangular field size. Can be symmetric or asymmetric.
Multi-Leaf Collimators (MLCs):
Many individually controlled leaves that conform the beam shape to the target.
Accessory Tray/Mount:
Holds wedges, custom blocks, or other beam modifiers[cite: 1318].
For electron therapy, the treatment head configuration changes:
The X-ray target and flattening filter are moved out of the beam path.
Scattering Foils:
One or more thin metallic foils are introduced to spread the narrow "pencil beam" of electrons into a broad, clinically useful beam.
Electron Applicators (Cones):

These attach to the treatment head and extend close to the patient's surface. They provide further collimation of the electron beam and define the final field size and shape at the skin[cite: 1318]. Standard sizes vary (e.g., 6x6 cm, 10x10 cm, etc.).
Ion chambers still monitor the electron beam.
Quick Check: In electron therapy, what is primarily used to spread the initial narrow electron beam?
Check Answer
Treatment Couch (PSA):
Supports the patient accurately and reproducibly. Often made of carbon fiber to minimize beam attenuation.
Capable of multiple movements: longitudinal (in/out), lateral (left/right), vertical (up/down), rotation, and sometimes pitch and roll.
Pendant controls
allow RTTs to move the couch from within the room[cite: 1317].
Indexed for precise attachment of immobilization devices.
Control Console:
Located outside the treatment room, RTTs operate the Linac from here.
Displays and allows setting of treatment parameters (MUs, energy, gantry/collimator angles, etc.)[cite: 1319].
Includes systems for
patient monitoring
(audio intercom and video cameras)[cite: 1320].
Features a complex
interlock system
that prevents beam delivery if unsafe conditions are detected.

pages.title: Lasers & Field Light - Guiding the Treatment

content.text: Laser System: [cite: 1318]
Essential for aligning the patient with the Linac's isocenter.
Typically includes:
Two
lateral (side) lasers
One
overhead (ceiling-mounted) laser
Sometimes a
sagittal laser
(projected along the couch or from the gantry).
These lasers define the three cardinal planes (axial/transverse, sagittal, coronal) intersecting at the isocenter.
Their accuracy is checked daily as part of QA.
Field Light:
A light source within the treatment head projects a beam of light that coincides with the shape and size of the radiation field.
Used by RTTs to visually align the radiation field with the patient's skin marks or setup landmarks.
The congruence between the light field and the radiation field is a critical QA check.

pages.title: Daily Warm-Up & Quality Assurance (QA) by RTTs

content.text: Before treating any patients each day, RTTs perform essential warm-up and QA procedures to ensure the Linac is operating safely and accurately.
Key Daily RTT QA Tasks:
Machine Warm-up:
Following the manufacturer's recommended procedures to bring the machine to stable operating conditions[cite: 1320].
Safety Interlock Checks:
Verifying that door interlocks, emergency stops, audio/visual monitors, and beam-on indicators are functional[cite: 1320].
Laser Alignment:
Checking that the room lasers accurately define the machine isocenter[cite: 1321].
Distance Indicator (ODI/Rangefinder):
Verifying its accuracy[cite: 1321].
Light Field vs. Radiation Field Congruence:
Ensuring the projected light field accurately represents the radiation beam (often checked with imaging)[cite: 1321].
Output Constancy Checks:
Verifying that the machine is delivering the correct radiation dose (often a simplified check by RTTs, with more detailed checks by physics).
All QA procedures and their results must be meticulously documented according to institutional policy.
RTTs must be proficient in handling emergency situations.
Emergency Stop Buttons:
Located on the Linac gantry, couch pendant, and control console. Pressing these will immediately terminate radiation and machine movement.
Responding to Events[cite: 1315]:
Equipment Malfunction (e.g., beam won't turn off, gantry stuck):
Hit emergency stop, safely assist patient, notify physics/engineering.
Power Failures:
Follow facility protocols for patient safety and machine shutdown. Many Linacs have battery backup for essential couch movements.
Fire:
Follow RACE (Rescue, Alarm, Contain, Extinguish/Evacuate).
Patient Movement or Needs Assistance:
Stop the beam (if on), use intercom to communicate, enter room if safe, address patient needs.
Understanding and practicing emergency shutdown and re-start procedures is critical[cite: 1322]. Safety interlocks (door, collision, etc.) are designed to prevent unsafe conditions.
Quick Check: If the Linac gantry begins to move unexpectedly towards the patient, what is the RTT's immediate action?

options: Press the nearest Emergency Stop button.
Try to manually stop the gantry.

content.text: Check Answer
This lesson provided an overview of the Linear Accelerator, covering its major systems, components, and the RTT's role in its operation, daily QA, and emergency preparedness.
Key Takeaways:
Linacs are complex devices requiring knowledgeable and skilled operators.
Understanding components from the drive stand to the treatment head is essential for RTTs.
Daily QA procedures ensure the Linac is functioning correctly and safely.
RTTs must be proficient in emergency procedures.
A thorough understanding of the Linac is fundamental to delivering safe and accurate radiation therapy.
